values.description: The clusters name who conducts intrusions - threat actor groups, intrusion sets, and curated lists of entities operating or selling intrusion capability.
The clusters name a bounded piece of intrusion activity - a campaign, an operation, a documented incident or case study against a specific target.
The clusters name malicious software families - ransomware, RATs, stealers, bankers, botnets, wipers and the like.
The clusters name software or services used in intrusions without being malware by design - dual-use and remote management tools, exploit kits, traffic distribution systems.

ATT&CK-shaped techniques whose clusters carry a kill_chain element naming their tactic, so they can be rolled up by tactic. A property of the sub-category, not something to infer from kill_chain_order.
Techniques from a framework with its own tactic vocabulary - DISARM, AM!TT, SPARTA, fraud frameworks and the like - which do not belong on one tactic strip with ATT&CK.
The clusters are the tactics themselves - the phases or goals of an intrusion - rather than the techniques used to reach them.
The clusters name an activity sector or industry that was hit.
The clusters name a place that was hit - a country or a region.
The clusters describe what was targeted when it is neither a sector nor a place - a kind of target or of targeted information.
The clusters are courses of action, mitigations and countermeasures addressing specific adversary behaviour.
The clusters are controls or requirements from a security control catalogue or assurance framework, not tied to a specific technique.
The clusters are detection rules ready to run against data - Sigma rules and the like.
The clusters are analytics and detection strategies - how a behaviour would be caught, rather than a rule ready to run.
The clusters name the data sources and data components a detection reads from.
The clusters name devices, equipment and infrastructure that can be exposed or attacked.
The clusters name platforms, such as operating systems.
The clusters name online services that can be exposed or abused.
The clusters name who produced the intelligence - the publisher of a report or a feed.
The clusters name organisations that appear alongside threat intelligence without being a threat themselves - vendors, agencies, institutions, listed entities.
The clusters name branded vulnerabilities - vulnerabilities known by a name rather than only an identifier.
The clusters are a reference list of sources used alongside threat intelligence - cited reports and publications, IP lists and the like.

description: The finer distinction inside a galaxy's category - actor vs malware within named-threat, for instance. Each value names its category of galaxy-category in parent; the reference category has none. Set on the galaxy definition, not on the cluster, and optional even when category is set.
author: MISP Project
